title: Economic strategy update and housing infrastructure funding
subtitle: Development charge cuts, doubled road resurfacing through the Building Faster Fund, and a draft water allocation policy
overview: At a special meeting, Council approved Make It Kitchener 2.1, a light update to the city's economic development strategy that will guide actions and investments from 2026 to 2030. It focuses on diversifying the economy and on a bolder vision for downtown, centred on arts and entertainment and an innovation district.

Council also agreed to apply to the provincial and federal Development Charge Reduction Program {{vote:m2}}. If the application is approved, the city would eliminate development charges on housing-enabling services such as roads, water, sewer and storm, and would seek matching grant funding for five growth projects. Staff said the plan is designed to break even without raising taxes or utility rates, but flagged risks, including growth forecasts and project delays.

Council further authorized an investment plan for the Building Faster Fund, which would fund the Hidden Valley culvert replacement and double the 2027 road resurfacing program. Staff said this takes resurfacing to about 9 kilometres.
The Mayor also announced that a draft Water Allocation Policy will return for Council's consideration on June 29.

decisions.detail: Council approved Make It Kitchener 2.1 as an update to the 2.0 strategy, to guide economic development actions and investments from 2026 to 2030.
Council delegated authority to the Chief Financial Officer to apply for the program and sign related agreements, contingent on the full grant funding being approved by the Province {{vote:m2}}.
Council delegated authority to the Chief Financial Officer to submit an investment plan covering the Hidden Valley culvert replacement and doubling the 2027 road resurfacing program.

debate: On Make It Kitchener 2.1, one councillor questioned whether diversifying the economy meant moving away from tech and was uneasy about the food incubator; staff said there is no intent to leave existing sectors and that food manufacturing is a job-growth opportunity, and staff will report back on limits under the Municipal Act.

Several councillors raised the defence focus and advanced manufacturing. One had concerns about community support for defence-related work and asked for engagement; another said local jobs from federal defence spending matter to many residents. Staff said the focus is on where tech and innovation align with defence, such as cybersecurity.

Councillors and a technology-sector delegate discussed retaining student talent, small equity stakes in grant-funded companies, and AI's effects on jobs and on electricity and water use. Some councillors called for bolder downtown investment and more housing in the core.

On development charges, one councillor questioned why the discount is the same across urban and suburban areas, and asked how benefits reach buyers. Staff said the program guidelines favour consistent rates, and that no condition can require developers to pass savings on to buyers.

A councillor who opposed the program called it risky, citing the report's statements that development charges are not believed to be a barrier to housing and that some administrative costs will not be recovered. Supporters said it avoids a tax increase and pays for hard infrastructure through development charges and grants.
